summary: This RFC is the formal specification of the Exterior Gateway Protocol, used between gateways of different autonomous systems in the ARPA Internet. It updates parts of RFC 888 and RFC 827. It is historic as a protocol now.

plainLanguage.summary: EGP let gateways exchange information about which networks they could reach. They acquired neighbors, checked whether those neighbors were reachable, and requested routing updates. RFC 904 is marked Historic.

subtitle: The Exterior Gateway Protocol's neighbor states, messages, and reachability exchanges.

tldr.problem: Gateways in different autonomous systems needed a precise procedure for finding neighbors, checking reachability, and exchanging network reachability information.
tldr.mechanism: EGP keeps a separate five-state machine for each neighbor. Request and Confirm acquire a neighbor, Hello and I-H-U monitor reachability, and Poll and Update exchange network information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 904 is marked Historic. It updates RFCs 827 and 888 and describes EGP as a protocol whose future growth could require revision or replacement.

today: RFC 904 is marked Historic. It updates RFC 827 and RFC 888; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What EGP Was Designed to Do
sections.content:
The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) exchanges network-reachability information between Internet gateways in the same or different autonomous systems. RFC 904 is a formal specification intended as a reference for implementation, testing, and verification.

The protocol uses periodic polling. Gateways use Hello and I-Heard-You (I-H-U) messages to monitor a neighbor and Poll commands to request Update responses with reachability information. The RFC updates RFCs 827 and 888.
sections.plainLanguage: EGP let neighboring gateways ask whether each other was reachable and request updated network information. This RFC records the message and state-machine rules for that exchange.

sections.title: The Neighbor State Machine
sections.content:
Each gateway runs a separate state machine for each neighbor. Its five states are Idle, Acquisition, Down, Up, and Cease. A Start event sends a Request and enters Acquisition; a Confirm moves the relationship to Down, and reachability indications can move it between Down and Up.

A Stop event sends Cease and enters Cease. The gateway retries that command until it receives Cease-ack or another Stop event. Receiving Cease causes a Cease-ack response and a return to Idle.
sections.plainLanguage: The state machine tracks whether a gateway has no relationship, is acquiring a neighbor, considers it down or up, or is ending the relationship. Messages and timers move it between these states.

sections.title: How Reachability Is Judged
sections.content:
EGP counts neighbor-reachability indications in a moving time window instead of treating one missed response as proof of failure. In active mode, a gateway sends Hello messages and counts I-H-U responses. In passive mode, it uses status information in received Hello or Poll messages.

The RFC suggests thresholds for declaring a neighbor up or down and provides suggested timer values, including P1 of 30 seconds for Hello intervals and P2 of 2 minutes for Poll intervals. These settings are suggested values; the document says they may not suit every configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway counts recent signs of reachability before changing a neighbor's state. This filters out brief interruptions that might otherwise cause unnecessary route changes.

sections.title: Messages and the Common Header
sections.content:
Every EGP message has a 10-octet header with version, type, code, status, checksum, autonomous-system number, and sequence number fields. The version value specified is 2.

Acquisition messages include Request, Confirm, Refuse, Cease, and Cease-ack. Reachability messages are Hello and I-H-U; Poll requests reachability data and Update returns it. Update messages list gateways and networks, with hop counts that the RFC says are not routing metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Every EGP message begins with fields that identify its type and the sending gateway's autonomous system. The message type shows whether the gateway is acquiring a neighbor, checking reachability, or exchanging updates.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: EGP version; the RFC specifies version 2.
